REDACT: A Systematically Controlled Multilingual Benchmark for Personal Information Detection

Guneesh Vats    Anubha Agrawal    Shikha Singhal    Ajita Dash Affiliation: Praison Selvaraj    Vidhan Jhawar    Ranga Prasad Chenna    Bharadwaj Y M G Affiliation: ServiceNow Affiliation: {guneesh.vats, anubha.agrawal, shikha.singhal, ajita.dash}@servicenow.com Affiliation: {praison.selvaraj, vidhan.jhawar, rangaprasad.chenna, bharadwaj.ymg}@servicenow.com
Abstract

Benchmark infrastructure for personally identifiable information (PII) detection remains limited: existing corpora cover few entity types, use ad hoc generation conditions, and do not show which surface conditions cause detector failures. We present REDACT, a systematically controlled multilingual PII benchmark with 13,42713{,}427 records, 324,078324{,}078 entity annotations, 5151 entity types, 4,1274{,}127 surface-form patterns, and 2525 languages across 99 scripts. A strength-2 covering-array sampler controls nine generation axes: domain, format, difficulty, length, density, code-switching, language, adjacency, and co-occurrence. Three entity-level metadata fields (disclosure status, disclosure form, and a GDPR-aligned sensitivity tier) enable stratified evaluation beyond aggregate or per-type F1. From the full benchmark, we evaluate five detectors (Presidio, GLiNER, the OpenAI Privacy Filter, GPT-4.1, and Claude Sonnet 4.6) on a locked, language-stratified sample of 1,0001{,}000 records. Aggregate F1 masks an architecture-dependent failure structure: the rule-based detector performs poorly on the highest-stakes data, including HIGH-sensitivity categories (recall 0.070.07) and non-verbatim disclosure forms, while the LLM detectors remain more robust, with the HIGH tier as their strongest sensitivity slice. A three-model reference-free LLM-as-judge assessment corroborates that sensitivity-tier assignment is the task’s hardest axis. We release the benchmark, schema, prompts, and stratified evaluation harness.

1 Introduction

Personally identifiable information (PII) detection in unstructured text is governed by data-protection regulation: the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (European Parliament and Council, 2016), the U.S. Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, and equivalent regimes in Brazil and Japan require organizations to identify and process identifiers from logs, chat transcripts, and customer-service records with documented accuracy. A detector that catches names but misses national identification numbers, handles English but not Hindi, or recognizes John Smith but not J.S. or [REDACTED] falls short along axes current benchmarks do not measure.

Three gaps in the current evaluation landscape motivate this work. First, existing PII benchmarks operate in narrow multilingual regimes: TAB (Pilán et al., 2022) and the i2b2/n2c2 challenges (Stubbs et al., 2017) cover only English; SPY (Savkin et al., 2025) covers two English domains; AI4Privacy (Ai4Privacy, 2025) spans 2323 languages but uses templated generation that limits behavioral diversity; and PIIBench (Jha, 2026) consolidates ten English sources into a unified taxonomy. This leaves practitioners with little evidence about how detectors behave under the multilingual, mixed-format, and compliance-sensitive conditions seen in deployment. Second, aggregate F1 is the dominant metric, yet high scores routinely mask severe per-entity failures (Fu et al., 2020); detectors can perform unevenly across entity types once the taxonomy is broad enough to expose those differences (Jha, 2026). What is missing is a systematic way to surface such failures along regulatorily meaningful axes. Third, no public PII benchmark records whether a mention is actually disclosed versus hypothetical, redacted, or only partially exposed, even though these distinctions determine real-world detector utility.

We introduce REDACT, a multilingual PII detection benchmark constructed to address these three gaps.11 1 All code, the generation, detector, and judge prompts, the quality rubric, and the evaluation harness are released at the anonymized repository: https://github.com/guneeshvats/REDACT-PII-Benchmark. Our contributions are: (1) a 5151-type PII taxonomy across 2525 languages with an explicit HIGH-sensitivity slice covering GDPR Article 9 special-category data, Article 10-style criminal-offence data, and linkage-risk identifiers (Section 3.1); (2) a nine-axis stratified sampler that exercises every pair of axis values via a strength-2 covering array (Kuhn et al., 2003) (Section 3.3); (3) three entity-level metadata fields (disclosed, disclosure_form, sensitivity_tier), inspired by privacy-oriented anonymization annotation in TAB (Pilán et al., 2022), powering a stratified-evaluation framework (F5 per disclosure form, F6 per sensitivity tier) that reveals detector failures aggregate F1 hides (Section 3.5); (4) a reproducible seven-stage generation pipeline with deterministic offset alignment, conditional verification, and a six-metric release-gate protocol (Section 3.4); and (5) an empirical evaluation of five detectors (Presidio (Microsoft, 2024), GLiNER (Zaratiana et al., 2024), the OpenAI Privacy Filter (OpenAI, 2026), GPT-4.1, Claude Sonnet 4.6) under partial, exact, and fuzzy span matching (Section 4).

2 Related Work

PII benchmarks. Existing PII resources make different coverage trade-offs. Real-text corpora such as the i2b2/n2c2 challenges (Stubbs et al., 2017) and TAB (Pilán et al., 2022) provide carefully annotated data, but they are limited to English and to a small number of domains. Synthetic and consolidated resources broaden the setting: AI4Privacy spans many languages (Ai4Privacy, 2025), SPY studies synthetic PII in two English domains (Savkin et al., 2025), and PIIBench consolidates English sources into a larger taxonomy (Jha, 2026). These benchmarks are useful, but they do not jointly provide broad multilingual coverage, fine-grained PII types, disclosure-form labels, and sensitivity-tier slices. Our benchmark is designed to fill this combined evaluation gap (Appendix H). TAB also motivates treating privacy annotation as more than span classification, since anonymization decisions depend on whether and how information should be masked. We build on that direction by recording disclosure status, disclosure form, and sensitivity tier at the entity level, then using those fields for stratified recall. Detector-side systems such as GLiNER2-PII (Zaratiana et al., 2026) and RECAP (Rajgarhia et al., 2025), as well as model-level privacy benchmarks such as PrivLM-Bench (Li et al., 2024), are complementary to this work because they can be evaluated using the substrate we provide.

Evaluation methodology. Our stratified metrics build on attribute-based NER evaluation (Fu et al., 2020) and behavioral testing (Ribeiro et al., 2020), applying them to PII attributes that matter for compliance. For construction, we draw on single-call data generation (Xu et al., 2024), iterative deduplication (Wang et al., 2023), and prior multilingual NER benchmarks (Malmasi et al., 2022; Fetahu et al., 2023) to set language and coverage targets.

3 Dataset Construction

We construct the benchmark to satisfy three operational requirements that prior PII corpora address only partially: (i) coverage across a broad multilingual taxonomy aligned with high-sensitivity privacy categories, (ii) stratification along axes that surface detector failure modes hidden by aggregate metrics, and (iii) reproducibility from a fixed catalog of 4,1274{,}127 PII patterns. The construction proceeds through a seven-stage record-generation pipeline after taxonomy and pattern-catalog specification: stratified plan generation, single-call LLM generation, deterministic span checking and offset alignment, conditional verification, repair, deduplication, and quality auditing.

3.1 Taxonomy

We define 5151 canonical entity types organized into seven families: identification, contact, demographic, geographic, financial, professional, and digital. All 5151 are listed in the per-type results (Appendix K, Figure 5), with the HIGH-sensitivity categories banded there. The 51-type granularity is finer than the approximately ten categories of TAB (Pilán et al., 2022) and broader than the 30-category schema of Jha (2026). We treat the HIGH-sensitivity types as a distinguished evaluation slice in Section 3.5.

3.2 Pattern Catalog

For each entity type and language we compile a catalog enumerating the surface forms an entity can take, assembled as the union of four annotators’ independent enumerations with rare and long-tail forms explicitly solicited (Appendix A): 4,1274{,}127 patterns across 2525 languages in three resource tiers (six high-, three mid-, and sixteen lower-resource languages; full list in Appendix G). Patterns carry country-specific identifier formats with checksum specifications (Luhn, IBAN mod-97, national-ID schemes), seven non-Gregorian calendar systems for Date_of_Birth, and locale-appropriate name distributions.

3.3 Nine-Axis Stratified Sampler

We define nine axes that, in combination, govern the distribution from which records are sampled: domain (1212 values), format (77 values), difficulty (33 values), length (44 values), density (33 values), code_switching (33 values), language (2525 values), adjacency (33 values), and co_occurrence_pattern (1515 patterns plus a sentinel). The full value set for each axis is enumerated in Appendix G. A naive full factorial over these axes would require 10,886,40010{,}886{,}400 records to realize every combination exactly once. We instead adopt a strength-2 covering array construction (Kuhn et al., 2003; Kuhn et al., 2010), which guarantees by design that every pair of axis values co-occurs in at least one planned record while reducing the planned sample by three orders of magnitude. After the quality filtering and deduplication described in Section 3.6, the released corpus realizes 98.2%98.2\% of all pairwise axis-value combinations across the (92)=36\binom{9}{2}=36 axis pairs. The remaining gap reflects records removed during filtering rather than missing combinations in the sampling plan.

The sampler additionally supports a paired-sweep mode that holds entity content fixed while a single axis varies, isolating that axis’s effect on detector behavior. We release this mode as part of the harness and discuss the quantitative analysis in the Limitations.

3.4 Generation Pipeline

Each plan row produced by the sampler is processed through a seven-stage pipeline (Figure 1) implemented atop the SyGra synthetic data generation framework (Pradhan et al., 2025). The generator (Stage 2) issues a single LLM call per record under a structured prompt of 1616 hard rules and 1010 few-shot anchors (Appendix D); a single call rather than a multi-step decomposition keeps all record-level constraints in one generation context (Xu et al., 2024). The offset aligner (Stage 3) performs deterministic span checking by recomputing character offsets with iterated str.find, so annotation integrity is checked before release rather than left to post-hoc manual inspection. The verifier (Stage 4) repairs flagged records with GPT-4o-mini, the deduplicator (Stage 6) applies an SBERT cosine pre-filter (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019; Gao et al., 2021) followed by ROUGE-L (Lin, 2004; Wang et al., 2023), and the auditor (Stage 7) computes the release gates of Section 3.6.

3.5 Metadata Fields

The core annotation design adds three metadata fields to each entity, beyond the standard type-and-span pair. These fields are inspired by privacy-oriented annotation in TAB (Pilán et al., 2022), but are operationalized here for multilingual stratified PII evaluation.

disclosed.

A boolean separating entities actually disclosed in the text from those mentioned hypothetically, counterfactually, or in denial (e.g., “if your accrual were 1.25 sick days per month”), so that behavior on non-disclosed mentions is scored rather than ignored.

disclosure_form.

A field over {complete, partial, obfuscated}: a fully spelled entity (“John Smith”), a truncated/initialed form (“J. Smith”, last four SSN digits), or class-preserving masking (“REDACTED”, “[NAME]”). Per-form recall reveals degradation on the non-verbatim forms central to enterprise deidentification.

sensitivity_tier.

A field over {HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW}. The HIGH tier includes GDPR Article 9 special-category data, Article 10-style criminal-offence data, and linkage-risk identifiers such as Date_of_Birth, which we mark HIGH because of its identity and linkage risk. MEDIUM covers direct identifiers outside this HIGH set, including names, account numbers, emails, phones, addresses, and similar IDs; LOW covers quasi-identifiers such as city, country of residence, and business title. Appendix E gives the decision rules used for ambiguous cases such as nationality versus country of residence, medical hints versus explicit medical information, and category mentions. Per-tier recall isolates the high-sensitivity subset that aggregate metrics dilute.

Validated by the auditor (Stage 7), these fields underpin the F5/F6 framework (Section 4). The contribution is their combined release and use as recall slices for multilingual PII evaluation, rather than any single metadata label in isolation.

3.6 Quality Assurance

We apply a release-gate protocol of six critical quality metrics: five for annotation integrity and one for coverage (Appendix B). After structural filtering, multi-mention and span repair, and near-duplicate removal (a further 4444 records), the released corpus contains 13,42713{,}427 records, corresponding to a 94.0%94.0\% retention rate (Figure 1). The auditor checks six release gates; five pass, and B4 (triple-name decomposition) is the only failing gate. Appendix B summarizes the gate definitions and pass/fail outcomes; the full auditor report is released with the harness.

3.7 Corpus Statistics

The released corpus comprises 13,42713{,}427 records and 324,078324{,}078 entity annotations (24.124.1 per record). Coverage is balanced: each of the 2525 languages contributes 453453–621621 records across 99 scripts, and each entity type appears in at least 5050 records. This allows per-type evaluation for all 5151 types, including HIGH-sensitivity. Records with at least one HIGH-sensitivity entity total 3,8293{,}829 (28.5%28.5\%). The corpus instantiates 51.9%51.9\% of catalog patterns and realizes 98.2%98.2\% of pairwise axis-value combinations; mean pairwise ROUGE-L is 0.030.03, confirming low residual near-duplication.

4 Evaluation Framework

We evaluate detectors on aggregate accuracy and on stratified recall along the two metadata axes introduced in Section 3.5.

4.1 Detector Baselines

We evaluate five detectors spanning the dominant deployment families. Microsoft Presidio (Microsoft, 2024) combines regular expressions with spaCy NER (Honnibal et al., 2020); GLiNER-multi (Zaratiana et al., 2024) is a zero-shot multilingual span detector run with sliding-window inference; the OpenAI Privacy Filter (OpenAI, 2026) is an open-weight fine-tuned token classifier emitting eight coarse categories mapped onto our taxonomy; and GPT-4.1 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 are frontier LLMs used as zero-shot extractors under identical instructions. All five run on a locked, language-stratified sample of 1,0001{,}000 records from the full corpus (Section 4.5), with native schemas mapped to our 5151-type taxonomy via the released catalogs.

4.2 Span Matching

We report micro- and macro-F1 under three modes: exact (coincident spans), partial (any same-type overlap), and fuzzy (≥50%\geq 50\% overlap of the shorter span). We use partial-overlap as the primary metric, following TAB (Pilán et al., 2022) and the de-identification literature (Stubbs et al., 2017), where boundaries may vary even when the detection decision is correct. LLM outputs require special handling because the prompts ask models to return entity strings and types, while character offsets are not always reliable. We therefore relocate each LLM prediction using occurrence-tracked str.find against the same input text. This step only maps the model’s emitted string back to a position; it does not change the predicted string or entity type, and predictions that cannot be located are left unmatched. Systems that emit native offsets are scored using those offsets. After this normalization, all predictions are evaluated with the same exact, partial, and fuzzy span matchers. This choice evaluates detection quality separately from output-format artifacts while keeping strict offset reliability visible through the exact-match setting.

4.3 Stratified Recall

The framework’s principal evaluation contribution is the stratified family, which decomposes aggregate performance along the two metadata axes of Section 3.5. Because disclosure form and sensitivity tier are properties of the gold entities, we stratify recall rather than F1: a prediction’s tier or form is defined only once it is matched to a gold entity, so precision is not attributable to a gold slice.

F5: per-disclosure-form recall.

For each detector, we compute recall separately on the subset of gold entities tagged complete, partial, and obfuscated. The obfuscation gap ΔF5=Rcomplete−Robfuscated\Delta_{\text{F5}}=R_{\text{complete}}-R_{\text{obfuscated}} quantifies the degradation that aggregate F1 hides; a large positive ΔF5\Delta_{\text{F5}} indicates that the detector relies on full surface forms and cannot generalize to redacted or truncated mentions.

F6: per-sensitivity-tier recall.

Analogously, we compute recall stratified by HIGH, MEDIUM, and LOW sensitivity tiers. The HIGH-sensitivity gap ΔF6=RLOW−RHIGH\Delta_{\text{F6}}=R_{\text{LOW}}-R_{\text{HIGH}} isolates regulatory-sensitive performance. A positive ΔF6\Delta_{\text{F6}} indicates a detector that underperforms on the HIGH-sensitivity categories carrying the highest legal stakes; as Section 5 shows, the sign of this gap is determined by detector architecture.

We additionally report per-entity-type F1 (51 rows) and per-language F1 (25 rows), extending PIIBench’s per-type failure-mode analysis (Jha, 2026) to a larger taxonomy and language set.

4.4 Prompts and Quality Assessment

Both detectors and judges use a final prompt revision with four-level rubric anchors, bias controls, few-shot exemplars (Brown and others, 2020), and an inline Article 9 mapping (all revisions are released with the harness). Beyond detector scoring we assess intrinsic record quality with a reference-free LLM-as-judge protocol after G-Eval (Liu et al., 2023), scoring each record 11–1010 on six weighted dimensions (realism, entity validity at 2.02.0; type, disclosed-flag at 1.51.5; tier, span quality at 1.01.0). The anchor ranges used by the judges are listed in Appendix F. A three-family panel (GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Pro) guards against single-vendor bias; Gemini returned valid scores on 348348 of 500500 records and the others on all 500500, each at its realized size, with inter-judge agreement by pairwise Cohen’s κ\kappa over three ordinal bins.

4.5 Sample Sizes and Statistical Power

Evaluation uses three nested samples: the detector sample (1,0001{,}000 records, 4040 per language, fixed seed), the quality panel (500500 records), and manual validation (510510 entities, 1010 per type, two annotators, plus a 2525-record audit). For manual validation, annotators independently checked each sampled entity against the generated text for type, span, disclosed flag, disclosure form, and sensitivity tier. The separate record-level audit checked whether any PII mentions in the sampled records were missing from the gold annotations. Per-language resolution is the binding constraint; Appendix C gives the sizing rationale.

5 Results

5.1 Aggregate Detector Performance

Table 1 reports aggregate performance on the locked 1,0001{,}000-record sample. Under the primary partial-overlap metric, Claude Sonnet 4.6 leads (0.6360.636), followed by GPT-4.1 (0.5970.597), the OpenAI Privacy Filter (0.5120.512), GLiNER (0.3200.320), and Presidio (0.1950.195). Macro-F1 and exact-overlap largely preserve this ranking; Presidio’s 0.0630.063 macro-F1 reflects near-zero recall on many types.

5.2 Stratified Evaluation: an Architecture-Dependent Failure Structure

Figure 2 shows the main value of the metadata slices: detector failures are not uniform, but depend strongly on architecture. On the sensitivity axis, Presidio drops from 0.230.23 recall on LOW-tier entities to 0.070.07 on the HIGH tier, giving an HIGH-sensitivity gap of ΔF6=+0.16\Delta_{\text{F6}}=+0.16. The non-regex systems show the opposite pattern: GLiNER, the OpenAI Privacy Filter, GPT-4.1, and Claude Sonnet 4.6 all reach their highest tier recall on HIGH entities (0.420.42, 0.570.57, 0.740.74, and 0.770.77). Thus, a single aggregate F1 score hides the specific slice where the rule-based system is least reliable. The Privacy Filter result should be read with one caveat: much of its HIGH recall comes through broad ID/account labels, while true HIGH-sensitivity categories such as religion remain difficult for its native schema.

The disclosure-form axis shows the same split. Presidio recovers 0.230.23 of complete mentions, but only 0.020.02 of partial and 0.070.07 of obfuscated mentions. GPT-4.1 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 handle partial mentions much better (0.780.78 and 0.840.84 recall), though obfuscated masks remain harder. Per-type and per-language results (Appendices K and I) show the same ordering: LLMs lead across all 2525 languages, Presidio is near-zero on HIGH-sensitivity and long-tail types, and name components remain weak.

5.3 Data Quality

Two independent checks support the synthetic gold. A three-judge G-Eval panel (GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Pro) gives a cross-judge weighted mean of 8.04/108.04/10 (Table 2); we treat this as a diagnostic check rather than ground truth. Two annotators manually validated 510510 entities (1010 per type) for type, span, disclosed flag, disclosure form, and sensitivity tier. Agreement with the gold is 99.1%99.1\% for type, 99.1%99.1\% for span, 99.7%99.7\% for disclosed flag, and 99.8%99.8\% for disclosure form; annotators also reach 96.4%96.4\% raw agreement with each other. A separate 2525-record audit covering 521521 entities finds a missed-entity rate below 3.3%3.3\%. Both checks identify sensitivity tiering as the hardest axis: it is the lowest-scored G-Eval dimension and the only annotation field with substantial human disagreement (90.5%90.5\% agreement, κ=0.25\kappa=0.25). We therefore treat tier-specific findings as central but bounded by the manual validation, explicit tiering rules, and stratified detector results.

6 Discussion

The central result is that aggregate F1 is insufficient for PII evaluation: Presidio’s 0.1950.195 partial-overlap micro-F1 masks a higher-risk failure, with HIGH-tier recall of only 0.070.07 versus 0.740.74 for GPT-4.1 and 0.770.77 for Claude Sonnet 4.6. Disclosure form shows the same pattern: Presidio recalls only 0.020.02 of partial and 0.070.07 of obfuscated mentions, while LLM detectors handle partial mentions more reliably. These slices matter because HIGH-sensitivity attributes and non-verbatim identifiers are precisely where aggregate metrics can make a detector look safer than it is. Because sensitivity tiering is also difficult (90.5%90.5\% agreement, κ=0.25\kappa=0.25, and the lowest G-Eval scores), future PII systems need both span detection & reliable risk-aware classification.

7 Conclusion

We presented REDACT, a systematically controlled multilingual PII benchmark with 13,42713{,}427 records, 324,078324{,}078 entity annotations, 5151 entity types, and 2525 languages. Its nine-axis covering-array design and entity-level metadata for disclosed status, disclosure form, and sensitivity tier enable stratified evaluation beyond aggregate F1. On a locked 1,0001{,}000-record sample, Claude Sonnet 4.6 leads partial-overlap micro-F1 (0.6360.636), followed by GPT-4.1 (0.5970.597), while the stratified results show that rule-based detection is weakest on HIGH-sensitivity and non-verbatim PII. We release the benchmark, schema, prompts, and harness to support more compliance-aware audits of PII detection systems.

Limitations

We describe five limitations of the present work and the follow-on work needed to address them.

Synthetic–real validity is not yet quantified.

The benchmark includes infrastructure for comparing detector rankings between synthetic and real PII data, but this paper does not report a validated correlation coefficient. The main obstacle is data coverage: public real-data PII corpora are much narrower than this benchmark in language, domain, and entity-type coverage. TAB (Pilán et al., 2022), for example, is English, legal-domain data with four NER-style categories. A correlation on that small overlap would test only that slice, not the full benchmark. The i2b2/n2c2 clinical corpora (Stubbs et al., 2017) are a natural next comparison, but they require a data-use agreement whose timeline did not permit inclusion.

Paired-sweep axis-effect analysis is deferred.

The sampler supports a content-controlled paired-sweep mode (Section 3.3) for isolating the effect of one axis at a time, but this paper does not report paired-sweep deltas. That analysis requires a separate controlled generation and detector run, so we release the mode and leave the quantitative axis-effect results to future work.

Detector experiments use sampled records.

All five detectors are evaluated on a locked, language-stratified sample of 1,0001{,}000 records from the full 13,42713{,}427-record corpus, mainly because frontier-model inference is costly. The sample is sized for aggregate and per-language comparisons, but estimates for the rarest entity types have wider intervals. We therefore report confidence intervals for headline comparisons.

HIGH-sensitivity results may depend on synthetic wording.

The LLM detectors’ strong recall on HIGH-sensitivity entities may partly reflect how clearly those categories are expressed in generated text. Religion, health, and orientation mentions often appear as distinctive content words, whereas identifiers such as account numbers may be embedded in strings. We therefore treat the HIGH-sensitivity inversion as a finding about this benchmark and detector set, especially Presidio’s weakness on this slice, rather than as a universal claim about all real-world HIGH-sensitivity data.

Triple-name decomposition remains difficult.

The one release gate the corpus does not fully clear is B4, which checks whether multi-component personal names are decomposed into their constituent mentions. Compliance is high for given-name and surname structures, but it degrades for naming systems with patronymics, compound surnames, or non-positional ordering. Locale-aware name decomposition is therefore a priority for the next catalog revision.

Ethical Considerations

The benchmark contains no real personal data. Every identifier is fabricated by the generator under an explicit fictional-content rule (R3, Appendix D): values are structurally plausible and satisfy real checksum and format specifications so that detectors behave realistically, but they correspond to no real individual. The resource is intended to evaluate and improve PII detection in support of data-protection compliance. We document where detectors fail, for example the rule-based weakness on HIGH-sensitivity categories, to prevent unsafe deployment rather than to enable evasion.

The released pattern catalog includes realistic surface forms and checksum-valid formats because such structure is necessary to test PII detectors. To reduce misuse risk, the release will include acceptable-use terms restricting the resource to research, evaluation, auditing, and defensive privacy work; it will prohibit attempts to use the catalog for impersonation, credential generation, evasion, or re-identification. The corpus itself exposes no real PII, but deployment of detectors trained or evaluated with it remains the responsibility of practitioners in their own legal jurisdictions. We release the corpus, schema, and harness for research use.

Appendix A Pattern Catalog Construction

The 4,1274{,}127-pattern catalog (Section 3.2) was compiled to maximize coverage of the surface forms each entity type takes across the 2525 languages. For every (entity type ×\times language ×\times surface-form class) cell, four annotators independently enumerated candidate patterns with the assistance of a large reasoning model (Claude Opus 4.6), each prompted to surface rare and long-tail realizations alongside common ones; we then retained the union of the four enumerations, so any pattern produced by any annotator is kept. Independent enumeration followed by union reduces the blind spots of any single prompt or annotator and is the basis for our coverage claim: the catalog is broad rather than exhaustive, since no finite catalog can enumerate every surface form a PII entity may take. Pattern validity is grounded in model-agnostic format specifications rather than in the enumerating model: country-specific identifiers satisfy real checksum schemes (Luhn, IBAN mod-97, national-ID), dates use the appropriate calendar system, and names follow locale-appropriate distributions. A pattern is therefore correct independently of how it was surfaced. The enumeration prompts, the per-annotator outputs, and the merged catalog are released with the benchmark.

Appendix B Release Gates

The release-gate protocol of Section 3.6 comprises six critical metrics. Five target annotation integrity: B1 (offset accuracy =100%=100\%), B2 (zero-entity rate ≤0.5%\leq 0.5\%), B4 (triple-name decomposition), B5 (canonical-type compliance =100%=100\%), and B6 (multi-mention completeness ≥95%\geq 95\%). One gate targets coverage, A2 (per-type record floor ≥50\geq 50).

Appendix C Sample Sizes and Statistical Power

Per-language resolution is the binding constraint on the 1,0001{,}000-record detector sample, which sits well above the Cochran floor for a ±5%\pm 5\% margin (Cochran, 1977). Manual-validation entities are judged independently by two annotators. The released evaluation harness supports confidence-interval estimation for headline comparisons; in this paper, we treat the 1,000-record detector run as a fixed, language-stratified evaluation sample.

Appendix D Generation Prompt

The Stage-2 generator is governed by a single structured prompt: a system message encoding the hard rules below, a user message carrying the fully resolved nine-axis configuration, and ten few-shot anchors covering the principal generation conditions (tight co-occurrence clusters, hypothetical/negated mentions, partial and obfuscated forms, OCR distortion, heavy code-switching, non-Latin scripts, and the paired-sweep mode). The model emits the passage and the entity list only; character offsets are computed downstream (Section 3.4). We summarize the rules here; the full prompt and all anchors are released with the benchmark.

R1.

Emit passage and entity strings only; no character offsets (computed downstream by deterministic alignment).

R2.

Every listed entity string appears verbatim in the passage (same casing, diacritics, script, whitespace).

R3.

All PII is fictional: plausible structure, fabricated content; no real people, numbers, or addresses.

R4.

One list entry per textual occurrence, not per distinct entity; repeated mentions each get an entry with an incrementing mention_index.

R5.

The passage satisfies all nine axis constraints at once; on apparent conflict the language axis is the matrix and code_switching the embedded language.

R6.

Adjacency (none/loose/tight) is the strongest structural constraint; tight follows the named co-occurrence (CO-###) template.

R7.

Each entity carries three semantic fields: disclosed (real disclosure vs. hypothetical/reported), disclosure_form (complete/partial/obfuscated), and mention_index.

R8.

OCR distortion uses realistic substitutions (l↔\leftrightarrow1↔\leftrightarrowI, O↔\leftrightarrow0, rn↔\leftrightarrowm, dropped diacritics, spacing and ligature errors); distorted strings are flagged obfuscated.

R9.

Code-switching is grammatical mixing within one passage (light == borrowings, heavy == phrase/sentence alternation, none == single language), not translation.

R10.

A pre-emission self-check verifies R2–R9 and R11–R16: verbatim presence, adjacency, occurrence counts, target-pattern presence, density-tier match, disclosed flags on hypothetical frames, triple-name decomposition, format validity, canonical-type membership, and disclosure-form consistency.

R11.

Triple-name rule: every Full_Name also emits nested First_Given_Name and Last_Family_Name spans, with locale-aware decomposition (Western, CJK, Hungarian, Spanish double-surname, Russian patronymic; particles kept with the surname, honorifics excluded).

R12.

Format-validity contract: the passage is machine-parseable in the requested format and generated identifiers satisfy their real-world checksum/format specs (Luhn, IBAN mod-97, country national-ID schemes).

R13.

All entity types are drawn from the 5151 canonical types only.

R14.

Sensitivity-tier and HIGH-sensitivity awareness: each entity is tiered HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW by regulatory sensitivity.

R15.

Script-aware definition of inter-entity spacing for non-whitespace-delimited scripts (CJK, Thai, Arabic), used by the adjacency check.

R16.

Frozen-entity pinning (paired-sweep mode only): supplied frozen entity values appear verbatim and are present in the output entity list.

Appendix E Sensitivity-Tier Decision Rules

Sensitivity tiers are assigned from the entity type and the disclosure context, not from detector confidence. Table 3 summarizes the operational rules used by the generator, judge prompt, and manual validation.

Appendix F Quality-Assessment Rubric

The reference-free LLM-as-judge protocol (Section 4.4) scores each record on a 11–1010 scale along six dimensions, each with four ordinal anchor levels. The six dimensions and weights are: realism (2.02.0), entity validity (2.02.0), type correctness (1.51.5), disclosed-flag correctness (1.51.5), tier correctness (1.01.0), and span quality (1.01.0). Table 4 gives the anchor ranges used in the judge prompt. The prompt also instructs judges to score each dimension independently, avoid penalizing synthetic text only because it is synthetic, avoid rewarding annotation volume, and apply the same HIGH-sensitivity / direct identifier / quasi-identifier tier mapping for all records.

Appendix G Sampler Axis Values

The covering array of Section 3.3 is constructed over the full value set of the nine axes, enumerated below so the sampling process is reproducible.

domain (12):

healthcare, legal, finance, education, government, technology, HR, insurance, customer_service, law_enforcement, social_media, e_commerce.

format (7):

plain_text, email, chat_transcript, ticket_worknotes, json_record, key_value_pairs, log_entry.

difficulty (3):

easy, medium, hard (extraction hardness).

length (4):

small (5050–200200 tokens), medium (200200–600600), large (600600–2,0002{,}000), very_large (2,0002{,}000–4,0004{,}000).

density (3):

low (11–44 entities / 11k tokens), medium (55–1515), high (≥16\geq 16).

code_switching (3):

none, light, heavy (grammatical language mixing within a record, not translation).

language (25):

AR (Arabic), CS (Czech), DA (Danish), DE (German), EN (English), ES (Spanish), FI (Finnish), FR (French), FR_CA (Canadian French), HE (Hebrew), HI (Hindi), HU (Hungarian), IT (Italian), JA (Japanese), KO (Korean), NL (Dutch), NO (Norwegian), PT_BR (Brazilian Portuguese), PT_EU (European Portuguese), RU (Russian), SV (Swedish), TH (Thai), TR (Turkish), ZH_CN (Simplified Chinese), ZH_TW (Traditional Chinese).

adjacency (3):

none (entities ≥10\geq 10 words apart), loose (33–1010 words), tight (a co-occurrence cluster).

co_occurrence_pattern (15 + sentinel):

CO-001 through CO-015, each a named dense-cluster template, e.g. CO-008 angle-bracket email metadata, CO-009 patient header, CO-010 authentication cluster, CO-011 compliance cluster, CO-012 HR record, CO-013 contact card, CO-014 legal citation, CO-015 form key-value adjacency, plus a none sentinel when adjacency ≠\neq tight.
